stories.title: Two people killed, 59 injured in explosion at military facility in Bolivia — TV
stories.summary: BUENOS AIRES, September 5. At least two people were killed and 59 injured in an explosion at a military barracks in the Bolivian municipality of Viacha, the Unitel TV channel reported, citing the local police. "Two people were killed, seven people are listed as missing, and 59 were injured," the TV channel quoted on its website Bolivia's deputy police chief Roger Roca as saying. According to Bolivia’s defense chief Ernesto Justiniano, six military personnel are among the injured, while the others are civilians. Rescue workers are continuing to operate at the scene. The explosion occurred in an area where "pyrotechnic materials" were stored, the defense chief said. Nearby houses were damaged by the blast wave.

stories.title: Is Russia proving better at protecting friends than fighting enemies in West Africa?
stories.summary: When mutinous soldiers seized a strategic military base in Niger's capital last Saturday, the country's ruling junta turned to a foreign partner it has increasingly relied on since coming to power: Russia. Following a night of intense fighting in Niamey, Russia's Africa Corps helped Nigerien loyalist forces to regain control of Air Base 101 at Diori Hamani International Airport. Africa Corps, unlike its predecessor the Wagner Group, is directly under the control of the defence ministry in Moscow. It provides combat support and military training and is thought to have some 200 to 300 men in Niger. Russia's ambassador to Niger, Viktor Voropaev, publicly acknowledged the weekend intervention, saying his country's forces had helped "repress a mutiny". "This is seen as a symbolic victory," according to Beverly Ochieng, senior analyst at Control Risks. "[One] that will continue to put them at the centre of not just the counter-insurgency campaign, but even in the protection and prolongation of military rule." The attempted coup offers perhaps the clearest evidence yet that Africa Corps' role in three Sahel countries extends beyond its stated mission of helping governments fight jihadist insurgencies. Russia is increasingly demonstrating that it can provide something perhaps even more valuable to the military rulers of Niger, Mali and Burkina Faso: protection for the governments themselves. "It was not sufficient to bring stability," said Ochieng, "but it's enough to allow these military governments to have a political lifeline." The thwarted mutiny also highlights something the ruling junta may not want to admit - just how dependent on Moscow it has become for security. In January, Africa Corps personnel also played an important role in repelling an attack at the same airport.
